governing_text: ParagraphPlan refines the document plan down to paragraphs: after the Brief, the Composer generates each Leg Waypoint's Paragraph Waypoints through the same kind of feedback loop as the Brief's, and hands them to the Packet through a planning record, never directly. Move information may be used up to Paragraph Waypoint generation and nowhere after it. It is not Reiter and Dale's microplanning: word choice, reference and sentence shape stay inside the one Writer call. [implemented-against: specs/spec-draft-pipeline/SPEC.md "The ParagraphPlan stage", copied 2026-10-14]
licensed_by: kogaki#1375 -- owner decision 2026-10-14: Paragraph Waypoint generation is its own stage after the Brief, named ParagraphPlan, with its own file and command; the ParagraphPlan file names the Brief it was made from and the Brief names nothing downstream; retries and limits follow the Brief's rules, `brief.call_limit_s` per call and `brief.unit_attempts` per unit, with no limit on the whole job.
shared_text_note: ONE CRITERION, WRITTEN ONCE (kogaki#1452): where the planner row and the judge row carry one criterion, it is written here and both `judgment_point` strings name it as `{{shared:<name>}}`; `judgePrompt` (src/workflow/judge.mjs) substitutes it, and checks/check-schema-binds.sh refuses a sentence one row carries with words changed from another's. The `relation` gap of kogaki#1446 sat in exactly such a difference.

shared_text.does_is_an_operation: A Segment's `does` is an OPERATION TO PERFORM, NEVER A POINT TO STATE: it says what the paragraph does with its part at that place -- concede, define, name a case, answer -- and the Paragraph Waypoint for that Segment is the part of the Leg Waypoint's `point` on which that operation is performed; a `does` restated with the subject filled in is not a part of the point.
shared_text.relation_is_not_content: A Segment's `relation` is how the Paragraph Waypoint stands to the one before it, and is never part of what the Paragraph Waypoint says: a point carrying the relation's wording, or a clause saying how it stands to the point before it, is not a part of the Leg Waypoint's point (kogaki#1446).
shared_text.own_leg_words: A PARAGRAPH WAYPOINT'S WORDS COME FROM ITS OWN LEG WAYPOINT (kogaki#1449): they come from its own Leg Waypoint's point and Claim -- no Claim rides in the input apart from the `point` it justified (kogaki#1382), so in practice from that `point` -- and never from another Leg Waypoint's `point` or `next_point`, nor from a term coined in planning: a term that appears in no part of its own Leg Waypoint's `point` is not a part of that point.
shared_text.join_is_a_type: A `join` is ONE WORD of a closed set naming how this Leg Waypoint's first Paragraph Waypoint stands to the paragraph before it (kogaki#1477), never a sentence: `consequence` -- this paragraph follows from what the previous one established; `grounds` -- this paragraph gives the reason for what the previous one asserted; `contrast` -- this paragraph sets its matter against the previous one's; `elaboration` -- this paragraph carries the previous one's matter further or in more detail; `summary` -- this paragraph draws the preceding paragraphs together; `none` -- this paragraph opens on its own matter and no connective is owed. The word names a relation and carries no content: whether and how it becomes a connective is the Writer's.

judge.note: Every job unit of this stage is a headless session, a `claude -p` child that runs with no tools, spawned by the shared Detached Job supervisor (src/workflow/detached-job.mjs) with the binary the start act resolved. `model` NAMES THE BRIEF'S SETTING, `brief.judge_model`, because the owner decided this stage follows the Brief's rules rather than carrying settings of its own. `KOGAKI_JUDGE_CLI` replaces the resolved binary FOR FIXTURES ONLY.

job.note: ONE JOB UNIT PER LEG, in Reader Path order, and the two bounds are the Brief's own settings (kogaki#1375): a call running past `brief.call_limit_s` is stopped and spends one attempt, a refused answer spends one, an unreadable answer is asked again without spending one, and a unit that has spent `brief.unit_attempts` stops naming its Leg and the Waypoint its last refusal named. There is no limit on the whole job. Each attempt makes two calls: `paragraph_plan_unit` binds a paragraph Move to every Leg Waypoint and generates its Paragraph Waypoints, and `paragraph_plan_judge_unit` judges them against the bound Move. A refusal of either is put back into the next attempt's prompt verbatim.

paragraph_plan_unit.note: The first call of every attempt (kogaki#1375). It carries the second-pass judgment kogaki#1359 put inside the compose job, moved out of it: the Move binding is judged here, after the Brief is adopted, and its result never reaches the Brief. `src/paragraph-plan.mjs` renders this row through the shared `judgePrompt` renderer up to the input marker and appends one Leg's own input below it; `validateParagraphPlanUnit` reads the answer.
paragraph_plan_unit.judgment_point: plan the paragraphs of ONE Leg -- `leg_you_must_plan` in the input -- in two steps for EACH of its Leg Waypoints, in order. FIRST, bind ONE paragraph Move from `paragraph_moves_you_may_bind` (each Move's contract rides there from its record, its `before` and `after` -- maps keyed by dimension in the record -- rendered one `dimension: sentence` line per dimension, and its `segments` given as one entry per Segment: `segment`, its number; `does`, the step's operation, in prose; and `relation`, its relation to the Segment before it, in prose, empty on Segment 1): a Move fits where its `before` holds in the state the reader is in when this Leg Waypoint begins -- the Leg's `reader_state_before` for the first, and for every later one the state the previous Leg Waypoint's bound Move leaves the reader in -- and where its `after` moves the reader toward the NEXT Leg Waypoint's `point` (it rides on each entry as `next_point`), or toward the Leg's `reader_state_after` for the last. The next Leg Waypoint is fixed, so bind with it in view. Where NO Move in the library fits a Leg Waypoint, say so with `move: null` and one sentence `why` naming what no Move's `before` or `after` could hold -- never bind the nearest one. WHERE A LEG WAYPOINT FIRST USES A TERM THE LEG INTRODUCES (kogaki#1497): `terms_this_leg_introduces`, read from the Leg's `introduces`, names each term the Leg brings to the reader, with its `meaning` -- `null` where the Leg gives none, and then the meaning is yours to give, in your own words, as this reader needs it -- and the reader holds none of them until a point gives it, a `coined` and an `established` term alike. Where a Leg Waypoint's `point` is the first in the Leg to use such a term, bind a Move that fits and has a Segment whose `does` defines or names, and the Paragraph Waypoint on that Segment carries the term with its meaning in its noun phrase -- "the fusion reactor called zebra", not "zebra" -- even where the Move serves another purpose. Where no Move in the library that fits has such a Segment and the point still uses the term, the Paragraph Waypoint that first uses it carries its meaning in apposition, in your own words -- "zebra, the fusion reactor this article names". Never add a sentence introducing the term beside the Move's Segments. SECOND, for every Leg Waypoint whose Move you bound, generate the PARAGRAPH WAYPOINTS of the one paragraph carrying it: one Paragraph Waypoint per Segment of the bound Move's `segments`, in the Move's order, from four inputs and nothing else -- the Leg Waypoint's own `point`, the bound Move's `segments`, `persona`, who the reader is and what they already know, and `terms_this_leg_introduces`, whose meanings only the Paragraph Waypoint that first uses a term carries, as FIRST says. A PARAGRAPH WAYPOINT IS A PART OF THE LEG WAYPOINT'S POINT: together, the Paragraph Waypoints of one Leg Waypoint say what its `point` says and nothing more. {{shared:does_is_an_operation}} It stands in the Segment's `relation` to the Paragraph Waypoint before it, and the part's content comes from the Leg Waypoint's `point` alone. {{shared:relation_is_not_content}} {{shared:own_leg_words}} A Paragraph Waypoint has the same shape as a Leg Waypoint: `point`, the proposition its paragraph makes, in the article's subject, in one sentence -- what the paragraph establishes, never how the reader is to feel, never a Segment's clause with the subject filled in, and never a sentence for the writer to copy -- and `serves`, the Strand ids of the Claims it serves, each one a Claim the parent Leg Waypoint serves; every Claim the parent serves is served by at least one of them. A Paragraph Waypoint that states what the paragraph is DOING to its reader -- announcing, defining rather than arguing, closing a list, leaving nothing open -- instead of a part of what the point says, is wrong, not merely stylistically off. ONE FORM IS NOT A PART OF THE POINT, AND IS DECLARED AS SUCH (kogaki#1448): where a Segment's `does` acts on the reader's READING rather than on the subject -- it announces, flags the material as hard, concedes difficulty, or signals a turn -- the point has nothing for that Segment to carry, and inventing a part for it (anticipating a later Segment's verdict or reason, say) is wrong. Its Paragraph Waypoint carries `performs` in place of `point` and `serves`: one sentence naming the operation alone, as the Segment's `does` names it, stating no point and carrying no clause stating what the reader then takes, expects, understands or does, since that is the operation's effect and the Writer's performance supplies it (kogaki#1485). Where a Segment's `does` operates on the subject -- define, state, apply, derive, contrast, name a case -- its Paragraph Waypoint carries a `point`, never `performs`. A `performs` Paragraph Waypoint serves no Claim: every Claim the parent serves is served by at least one `point` Paragraph Waypoint, and a Leg Waypoint carries at least one. THIRD, for every Leg Waypoint AFTER THE FIRST whose Move you bound, choose its `join` from four inputs and nothing else: the state the previous Leg Waypoint's bound Move leaves the reader in (its `after`, the question or expectation it leaves), the previous Leg Waypoint's Paragraph Waypoints, this Leg Waypoint's bound Move, and this Leg Waypoint's first Paragraph Waypoint. {{shared:join_is_a_type}} Choose the word this first Paragraph Waypoint bears toward the paragraph before it, not the one the previous `after` asks for: a paragraph may answer a question later than the reader raised it, and where it defers what that `after` leaves open, the word is `contrast` or `none`. The FIRST Leg Waypoint of the Leg carries NO `join` -- the connection between Legs is the Brief's, not this stage's (kogaki#1411). Word choice, reference and sentence shape are NOT planned here; they stay with the Writer. The Leg's `reader_state_before` and `reader_state_after` decide which Move fits where, and are never stated in a Paragraph Waypoint or a join (kogaki#1452).
paragraph_plan_unit.input_shape: ONE plan record AT THE RECORD'S OWN ROOT -- `version` "1", the `leg_id` of the Leg in the input, and `waypoints`, one entry per Leg Waypoint in order: `{ "waypoint": <its 1-based number>, "move": <a Move id from the library, or null>, "why": <one sentence>, "join": <one word: consequence | grounds | contrast | elaboration | summary | none>, "paragraph_waypoints": [ { "point": <one sentence>, "serves": [<Strand id>, ...] } | { "performs": <one sentence: the Segment's operation on the reader's reading, in your words> }, ... ] }` -- `paragraph_waypoints` empty only where `move` is null, and carrying at least one `point` entry where it is not; `performs` stands in place of `point` and `serves` only for a Segment whose `does` acts on the reader's reading (kogaki#1448); `join` on every Leg Waypoint after the first whose Move is bound, and absent from the first
paragraph_plan_unit.refusal: a record naming another leg_id; `waypoints` not one entry per Leg Waypoint, or out of order; a key the record does not declare; a `move` naming no Move in the library; a `why` under four words; a Leg Waypoint whose Move is bound and which carries no Paragraph Waypoint; a Paragraph Waypoint with an empty point, an empty `serves`, a `serves` naming a Claim its parent Leg Waypoint does not serve, or any key but `point` and `serves` -- or, for a `performs` Paragraph Waypoint, an empty `performs` or any key beside it (kogaki#1448); a Leg Waypoint none of whose Paragraph Waypoints carries a `point`; a Claim the parent serves that no Paragraph Waypoint serves; a `join` on the first Leg Waypoint, or a Leg Waypoint after the first whose Move is bound and which carries no `join`, an empty one, or one that is not one word of the set (kogaki#1477); a Paragraph Waypoint whose content is not recoverable from the Leg Waypoint's `point` -- stating what the paragraph does to its reader instead of a part of what the point says -- named by its number and why. `move: null` is a judgment, not malformed output: the unit is refused `no_paragraph_move_fits` naming the Leg and the Waypoint, and asked again with the sentence until `brief.unit_attempts` is spent. A BOUND MOVE THAT DOES NOT FILL A ROLE THIS STAGE NEEDS (`before`, `after`, `segments` or `breaks`) is not a refusal of your answer: the stage stops, naming the Move and the role, and nothing is defaulted. The next attempt receives the refused record beside its refusal, both verbatim (kogaki#1438).
paragraph_plan_unit.governing: SPEC-draft-pipeline, the ParagraphPlan stage and the Move boundary; kogaki#1375

paragraph_plan_judge_unit.note: The second call of every attempt (kogaki#1375), run by the supervisor's judge phase once `validateParagraphPlanUnit` has passed the first call's record. `src/paragraph-plan.mjs` renders this row through `judgePrompt` up to the input marker; `paragraphPlanJudgePrompt` appends the Leg's input and `paragraphPlanJudgeVerdict` reads the answer. A `does-not-fit` on any Leg Waypoint is a refusal of the attempt, and its sentence is put into the next attempt's first call.
paragraph_plan_judge_unit.judgment_point: judge the Paragraph Waypoints of ONE Leg -- `leg_you_must_judge` in the input -- one verdict per Leg Waypoint, against the paragraph Move bound to it, whose `before`, `after`, `segments` and `breaks` ride on the entry from its record, `before` and `after` rendered one `dimension: sentence` line per dimension: the Leg judge's own four things (kogaki#1378, owner decision 2026-10-14), plus three more. FIRST, whether the Paragraph Waypoints, read in order, begin from a state the Move's `before` holds -- the Leg's `reader_state_before` for the first Leg Waypoint, the state the previous one's Move leaves the reader in for every later one. SECOND, whether they end where the Move's `after` leaves the reader, moving toward the entry's `next_point` (the Leg's `reader_state_after` for the last). THIRD, whether, read in order, they follow the Move's order as its `segments` give it, one Paragraph Waypoint per Segment (kogaki#1412). FOURTH, whether they survive each test in the Move's `breaks`. FIFTH, whether each Paragraph Waypoint's content is recoverable from the Leg Waypoint's own `point`: a Paragraph Waypoint is a part of that `point`. {{shared:does_is_an_operation}} {{shared:relation_is_not_content}} {{shared:own_leg_words}} So a Paragraph Waypoint that instead states what the paragraph does to its reader (announcing, defining rather than arguing, closing a list, leaving nothing open), or restates a Segment's `does` with the subject filled in, or carries its Segment's `relation` as content, does not fit, however well it tracks the Segment; and a Paragraph Waypoint carrying a term from outside its own Leg Waypoint's `point` -- another Leg Waypoint's term, or one coined in planning -- does not fit either, judged against that `point`. AND ITS COMPLEMENT (kogaki#1497): `terms_this_leg_introduces`, read from the Leg's `introduces`, names the terms the Leg brings to the reader, with their meanings; the first Paragraph Waypoint in the Leg whose `point` uses one of them gives its meaning -- in the noun phrase of a Segment that defines or names, or in apposition -- and a Paragraph Waypoint that first uses an introduced term and gives no meaning for it does not fit, its `why` naming the Paragraph Waypoint and the term. A meaning in the planner's own words fits as well as the input's, and where the input's `meaning` is `null` the planner's words are the only meaning there is, so judge whether a meaning is given, never whether it matches. The meaning carried there is the term's own and not a term from outside the point, and a `coined` and an `established` term are judged alike. SIXTH, each Paragraph Waypoint against ITS OWN Segment -- the Nth Paragraph Waypoint against the Move's Nth Segment: whether it is a part on which that Segment's `does` can be performed, and whether it stands to the Paragraph Waypoint before it in that Segment's `relation`, judged by the two points' order and dependence -- what this point takes from the one before it -- and never by wording inside a point; a Paragraph Waypoint that neither performs its Segment's `does` nor sits in its `relation` -- a first point unrelated to Segment 1's `does`, as on the 2026-10-16 run, where Segment 1 conceded the distinction was hard and promised to simplify it and the first point stated an unrelated fact -- does not fit, however true it is of the Leg Waypoint's `point`. UNDER SIXTH, TOO, A PARAGRAPH WAYPOINT'S FORM AGAINST ITS SEGMENT (kogaki#1448): a Paragraph Waypoint carrying `performs` in place of `point` declares that its Segment acts on the reader's reading and carries no part of the point; a `performs` Paragraph Waypoint for a Segment whose `does` names an operation on the SUBJECT (define, state, apply, derive, contrast) does not fit, because that Segment carries a part of the point; and a `point` Paragraph Waypoint for a Segment whose `does` acts on the READING (announce, flag, concede difficulty, signal a turn) does not fit, because its content is not a part of the Leg Waypoint's point but one the planner supplied. A `performs` Paragraph Waypoint is judged on whether its operation is its Segment's, never against FIFTH, which judges `point` Paragraph Waypoints only. And a `performs` Paragraph Waypoint that carries a clause stating the reader's resulting reading -- a "so that", an "in order that" or an equivalent stating what the reader then takes, expects, understands or does -- does not fit, because that is the operation's effect and the Writer's performance supplies it; its `why` names the entry and the clause (kogaki#1485). Where the Move carries no `segments`, SIXTH holds by default. SEVENTH, on every Leg Waypoint after the first, its `join` (kogaki#1411, kogaki#1477): whether its type is one the previous entry's bound Move's `after` admits and this entry's first Paragraph Waypoint bears. {{shared:join_is_a_type}} A paragraph may answer a question later than the reader raised it: where this entry's first Paragraph Waypoint defers what the previous `after` leaves open, `none` and `contrast` fit, and a join is never refused for not taking up that `after`. A type the first Paragraph Waypoint does not bear -- `consequence` where it does not follow from the previous paragraph, `grounds` where it gives no reason for it, `summary` where it draws nothing together -- does not fit, and its `why` names the join and the type the first Paragraph Waypoint bears. The first Leg Waypoint carries no join, and SEVENTH holds there by default. The bound Move's `before`, `after` and `breaks`, the Leg's `reader_state_before`, `reader_state_after` and `introduces`, and each entry's `join` are what you judge, never what your record states: it carries one verdict and one sentence per Leg Waypoint (kogaki#1452). Verdict `fits` only where all seven hold, `does-not-fit` where any does not, with one sentence `why` naming the Paragraph Waypoint, or the join, and the criterion it fails. Judge the points, not the Claims; how many Paragraph Waypoints there are is not judged.
paragraph_plan_judge_unit.input_shape: ONE verdict record AT THE RECORD'S OWN ROOT -- `version` "1", the `leg_id` of the Leg in the input, and `verdicts`, one per Leg Waypoint in order: `{ "waypoint": <its 1-based number>, "verdict": "fits" | "does-not-fit", "why": <one sentence> }`
paragraph_plan_judge_unit.refusal: a record carrying no `verdicts` array, or naming another leg_id; a verdict outside the closed set; a Leg Waypoint carrying no verdict, or two, or verdicts out of order; a `why` under four words -- each of these is this judge's own malformed output, and the same prompt is asked again. `does-not-fit` is a verdict, not malformed output: the attempt is refused with it and the plan is generated again. The next attempt receives the refused record beside its refusal, both verbatim (kogaki#1438).
